I often use find to locate certain types of files within a certain directory, e.g. "find some/dir/ -type f -name '*.jpg'" to find all .jpg files in 'some/dir/'. Grep is great for filtering output of some other command; I often use it with the -v flag to exclude results.

Sed and awk get into more complex manipulation of the stream, but are invaluable when other tools just won't cut it (pun intended). Locate is, if you have an appropriate indexing daemon running, a fast way to find a filename pattern anywhere on your filesystem.

Stringing these various tools together enables very powerful expressions right on the command line. For example, today I wanted to run jshint (a code checker) on all '.js' files in a directory unless the pathname contained 'node_modules', so I ran this:

$ find some/dir/ -type f -name '*.js' | grep -v node_modules | xargs jshint

And voila!

The inaugural review: Review #1 Chivas Regal 12 year old Blended Scotch

Chivas Regal 12 year old Blended Scotch Whisky

thedersy1's first review

This review is copied over from the one I did over at /r/scotch on Reddit, I wanted to help populate this place with some reviews!

Beginner to scotch, this is the first and only blend to come into my possession, also the first scotch to cross my lips and launch me into a bit of an obsession these past several months. I now feel that I am to the point where I can organize my thoughts coherently and cohesively. First on the table is the Chivas Regal 12 year, entry level offering from Chivas Brothers, and from what I understand, mostly comprised of Strathisla.

40% ABV, served into a glencairn, few drops of water.

Color: Golden amber.

Nose: Dry heat, cooked apples, dried fruits, apricots and raisins, maybe.

Palate: Apple pie, light toffee notes, spice, lightly oily mouthfeel, cereal

Finish: white pepper, medium length, drying.

Development: oily mouthfeel disappears, pepper and spice becomes more intense.

79/100

A solid blend at a solid price ($26 @ 750ml). At first not a very complex dram, but if you dig for it those sweet fruity notes begin to develop into several more distinct fruit notes (apple, apricot, raisins). I'd recommend this as a solid budget blend to any fruit fans. Would I buy another bottle? Not quite yet, I'm just beginning my malt journey and I have many more things to try before I circle back and purchase repeat bottles, but I would definitely consider it at a later point, it definitely has me interested about the 18yr offering.

What's to come: Now that I have a better sense of confidence in my nose and in my palate I'm going to be launching into more reviews, in the order in which the bottles were acquired. In this order will come the following reviews: Glenmorangie 10, Balvenie 12 DoubleWood, Macallan 12, Jura Collection (Jura 10 Origin, Superstition, Diurach's Own 16yr), and lastly (as of now) the Glenlivet Nadurra 16 year old. Until next time, cheers!

From the Aether site:

“Distributed” Think of Facebook. It is, for our purposes, a giant, powerful computer, a server, to which people connect to by typing to their browsers www.facebook.com. If, say, Alice wants to send a message to her friend Rachel over Facebook, Alice's message will first traverse Facebook, which will notify Rachel to come claim her message. This works reasonably well under most cases.

Now, imagine Rachel lives in Eastasia, a country equally famous for bad upper lip facial hair fashions and a tendency to block what it doesn't like to hear. Naturally Facebook and Twitter is blocked. Rachel and Alice are not blocked from each other, but since Facebook and Twitter, their venues of communication, is out, they can't talk. Rachel misses Alice.

Aether, in response to such a possibility, entirely does away with the middle–man, and links Alice and Rachel directly together. Now, when Rachel wants to send a message to Alice, she just rings her. The world is full of people in their situation, so if the line between them gets blocked, Rachel will just leave a message to one of their mutual acquaintances, perhaps to all of them, for Alice to claim. Each of these people will repeat this step. A thousand strangers allow Rachel practically infinite amount of potential paths to Alice.

To improve even more on the inevitability, Aether does not send messages for delivery to a single target, instead it sees to that the message will be delivered to all computers within Aether. Naturally, everything is public. Aether is a massive auditorium, not a private message delivery service.

Consequently, all information contained within are distributed across all users' computers. This makes Aether very hard to block. Removing the information published is comparable to removing a drop of ink from a glass of water after it is dropped. This is what “distributed” means.
